LOMAMO Foundation Kenya served 512 patients across 10 ministry areas in Kisumu and Homa Bay counties during January–June 2026 — enrolling 378 new patients, discharging 315, and recording 19 deaths (96.3% survival rate). The Foundation rescued 408 children from becoming orphans (94.4% prevention rate), saw 93 patients accept Christ, distributed 105 Bibles, and served 121 TB patients — reflecting intensified case-finding that drove a 72.9% year-on-year increase in TB detection while mortality fell.

Three new Homa Bay ministries (Shauri Yako, Makongeni, Sofia) launched in February served 92 patients in their first five months. Compared to the first half of 2025, every tracked indicator improved: enrolment +44.8%, discharges +41.3%, Bible distribution +84.2%. Nyalenda led in caseload (78) and salvations (19); Ahero led in children rescued (72).

Financially, the Foundation closed the half-year within its combined budget: KES 14,737,539 spent against a KES 14,772,049 budget — a saving of KES 34,510 while serving 512 patients (see Section 13).

2. Organisation Background

LOMAMO Foundation Kenya is currently operating 10 ministry areas — seven established in Kisumu County (Nyalenda, Manyatta, Nairobi Road, Ahero, Chiga, Nyahera, Ombeyi) and three new in Homa Bay County (Shauri Yako, Makongeni, Sofia, launched February 2026).

The Foundation's three-pillar mission is delivered through home-based care, hospital linkage, nutritional support, adherence counselling, and spiritual ministry by 15 staff (12 Kisumu, 3 Homa Bay) and 5 casual workers (3 Kisumu, 2 Homa Bay).

Interpretation: Every indicator improved. Largest gains: Bible distribution (+84.2%), TB case detection (+72.9%), and enrollment (+44.8%) — driven by stronger referral partnerships, expanded outreach, and the new Foundation vehicle. Concerns: the 11.8% rise in deaths and 76.9% rise in children orphaned reflect more patients presenting with advanced illness before enrollment. Of 23 children orphaned, 10 were referred to CHI. Structural conditions in informal settlements (overcrowding, poor ventilation, poverty, substance abuse) sustain TB transmission independent of ministry performance.

Total TB Patients12123.6%
Total HIV/AIDS Patients39176.4%

Why TB numbers rose (+72.9%): The increase reflects intensified case-finding, not worsening care. Three drivers: (1) strengthened CCC referral partnerships channeling more TB patients into home-based care; (2) enhanced community screening by caregivers and CHVs in informal settlements; (3) structural conditions — overcrowding, poverty, poor ventilation — sustaining transmission independently. That mortality simultaneously fell confirms better detection, not declining quality.

10. Factors Affecting Performance

Structural / External (not quality-dependent)

  • High disease burden — poverty, overcrowding sustain HIV/TB
  • Seasonal flooding restricting home-visit access
  • Patient stigma, discrimination, adherence choices
  • Fuel/food inflation increasing operational costs
  • Alcoholism & substance abuse → treatment interruption
  • Long distances in rural Homa Bay reducing visit frequency
  • Poor road infrastructure limiting emergency response

Within Ministry Influence

  • Home-visit frequency & consistency → adherence, discharge timing Positive impact — first half
  • Adherence counselling & health education quality Positive impact — first half
  • Discharge planning & patient education for lasting recovery Positive impact — first half
  • Spiritual care engagement & Bible distribution (varies by ministry) Positive impact — first half
  • CHV deployment & supervision — frontline case-finding Positive impact — first half
  • Referral coordination speed with health facilities Mixed impact — positive & negative

Reading: Five of the six factors within ministry influence — home-visit consistency, adherence counselling, discharge planning, spiritual care engagement, and CHV deployment — positively impacted first-half-year performance. Referral coordination speed with health facilities cut both ways, impacting performance both positively and negatively.

12. Partnerships, Challenges & 2026 July–December Priorities

Partnerships

JOOTRH, Kisumu County Referral Hospital, Kowino Dispensary, Nyalenda Health Centre, and various CCCs remain core referral partners. New collaboration with Homa Bay County Government creates opportunities for stronger referral systems and health-sector partnerships.

Challenges

  • Seasonal flooding: flooding during the rainy season restricted access to several villages, disrupting patient follow-up and service delivery.
  • Price inflation: rising market prices in fuel and food.
  • Poor road infrastructure: inaccessible roads and long travel distances increase operational costs, reduce productivity, and limit timely patient follow-up.
  • Transport gap: a single vehicle is insufficient for village-area operations.
  • Growing disease burden — particularly TB within informal settlements.
  • Huge patient referrals (care demand) with limited budgetary allocation; the capacity to serve patients is currently limited.

July–December Strategic Priorities

  • Accelerate Homa Bay — expand outreach, referrals, local partnerships.
  • Unlock field capacity — plan for additional 4×4 vehicle.
  • Establish LOMAMO Care Centre — short-term residential care for critically ill.
  • Upgrade data systems — track discharge reason, cause of death, TB type.
  • Improve local resource mobilisation — build on KES 302,373 raised in the first half of the year.

Target view: Kisumu discharges (54%) on track. Children rescued (42% Kisumu, 28% Homa Bay) need acceleration. Overall discharges (48.5%) likely achievable; children rescued (38.9%) is the July–December priority. Homa Bay's February start explains slower ramp — growth expected as ministries mature.

Kisumu (7 ministries, 12 staff): 420 patients (82.0%). Homa Bay (3 ministries, 3 staff): 92 patients (18.0%) in 5 months — per-ministry average of 30.7 compares well with early Kisumu trajectories.

100% prevention: Nyalenda, Ahero, Chiga. Outlier: Ombeyi — 12 orphans (73.3% rate, 52.2% of Foundation total). Foundation-wide 94.4% rate: ~1 orphan per 18 at-risk children. Target: 96%+ in July–December.

Financial reading: Homa Bay's under-spend (−KES 647,592) reflects its phased February launch and offset Kisumu's over-spend (+KES 613,082), leaving the Foundation KES 34,510 under budget overall. 14. Recommendations & Conclusion

Recommendations

  1. Procure an additional vehicle to support ministry work.
  2. Establish a budget for partnerships.
  3. Upgrade office technology.
  4. Acquire land for sustainability projects.

Conclusion

The first half of 2026 demonstrated strong organisational performance: every tracked indicator improved year-on-year — enrolment +44.8%, discharges +41.3%, TB detection +72.9%, Bible distribution +84.2%, salvations +32.9%. The survival rate (96.3%) and orphan prevention rate (94.4%) reflect the quality of LOMAMO's holistic care model, and the Foundation delivered this expanded impact while remaining within its overall budget. The Homa Bay expansion, while ramping up, has laid solid foundations.

Challenges remain — seasonal flooding, price inflation, poor road infrastructure, the transport gap, and a growing disease burden amid high care demand. With strengthened partnerships, expanded outreach, and the commitment of 15 staff and community health volunteers, the Foundation enters July–December well positioned to achieve its annual strategic objectives.

With God's guidance and the continued support of the Board, partners, donors, and volunteers, LOMAMO Foundation Kenya is equipped to deepen its impact among the vulnerable communities it serves.
